learn.title: Divide, sort, combine
learn.body: The three sorts so far are all $O(n^2)$ in the worst case. Merge sort does better with a different idea. Split the array in half, sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves into one sorted array.

learn.title: Merging is easy
learn.body: Merging two sorted lists is cheap. Look at the front item of each list and take the smaller one. Repeat. For {1, 4, 7} and {2, 3, 9} you take 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 and then 9. One pass, no backtracking.

learn.title: Splitting 8 items
learn.body: Keep halving until each piece has 1 item. A single item is already sorted.
steps: Each 4 splits into 2 and 2, so we have four pieces of 2
Each 2 splits into 1 and 1, giving eight pieces of 1
That is 3 levels of splitting. Then merge back up, level by level

learn.title: Why it is fast
learn.body: Splitting n items in half reaches single items after about $\log n$ levels. Merging at each level touches every item once, which is about n work. Total: $n \cdot \log n$ steps. For n = 8 that is 8 times 3 = 24.

learn.title: How big is the saving
learn.body: For n = 1024, $n \log_2 n$ is 1024 times 10, which is 10,240 steps. Compare that with $n^2$, which is 1,048,576. Merge sort is about 100 times less work at that size. The gap keeps widening as n grows.
Merge sort sorts by solving a smaller version of the same problem. The next unit explores that idea, called recursion.

questions.prompt: What are the three parts of merge sort?
questions.explanation: It divides the problem, solves the halves and combines the answers.

questions.prompt: Merging {1, 4, 7} and {2, 3, 9}. Which item is taken first?
questions.explanation: Compare the fronts 1 and 2 and take the smaller, 1.

questions.prompt: How many levels of splitting does an array of 8 items need to reach single items?
questions.explanation: 8 becomes 4, then 2, then 1. That is 3 halvings.

questions.prompt: Merge sort takes about $n \log n$ steps, which is far fewer than \_\_ for large n.
questions.explanation: The quadratic sorts do work that grows like $n^2$.

questions.prompt: For n = 8, how many steps is $n \log_2 n$?
questions.explanation: log base 2 of 8 is 3, and 8 times 3 is 24.

questions.prompt: Put the merge sort stages in order.
steps: Merge the sorted halves into one
questions.explanation: The halves must be sorted before they can be merged.

questions.prompt: Why is merging two sorted lists quick?
choices: Only the front items need comparing
questions.explanation: The smallest remaining item is always at the front of one of the two lists.
